Society · Demography · Data

Japan lost 530,000 people. Its foreign population grew by 325,000.

The latest official estimate shows one country moving in two directions. Immigration is changing daily life faster than the headline suggests—but it is not cancelling Japan’s demographic arithmetic.

By Yuji Shimizu · YUJI @ Japan
Published October 21, 2026 at 08:10 JST · 9 min read

Japan’s population was estimated at 122.69 million on October 1, 2026. That is 530,000 fewer people than one year earlier—roughly the population of a medium-sized Japanese city removed from the national total in twelve months. The figure, published by the Statistics Bureau on October 20, extends a decline that is now so familiar it can sound almost abstract.

But the same release contains a second movement. In the final estimate for May 1, the Japanese population had fallen by 855,000 year on year, while the foreign population had risen by 325,000, or 8.9%. Those two changes net to the same 530,000 decline reported for that May reference point. They are not a side note. They show that Japan is becoming smaller and more internationally diverse at the same time.

122.69mtotal population, Oct. 1 preliminary
−530,000total year-on-year change
+8.9%foreign population, May final

For every 100 people lost from the Japanese population over the year to May, the foreign population added about 38. Japan still shrank—but the country that remained became different.

The dates matter

Population releases can invite false precision, so the labels deserve attention. The 122.69 million headline is a preliminary estimate for October 1. It uses the latest available components and may be revised. The detailed Japanese and foreign totals are final estimates for May 1: 118.838 million Japanese nationals and 3.974 million foreign nationals.

That timing gap means readers should not subtract May’s nationality totals from October’s overall total. The responsible comparison is within each reference date. For May, the total was 122.812 million, down 530,000; the Japanese-national decrease and foreign-national increase explain that May change exactly. October supplies the freshest headline, while May supplies the detailed anatomy.

The age story is even harder

Nationality is only one axis. Age is the more stubborn constraint. In May, Japan had 13.263 million children under 15, down 353,000 from a year earlier, a fall of 2.6%. The working-age group from 15 to 64 numbered 73.322 million, down 200,000. People aged 65 or older numbered 36.227 million and edged up by 24,000.

Inside that older group, the 75-and-over population rose by 476,000 to 21.564 million—an increase of 2.26%. In other words, the broad 65-plus total barely moved because younger cohorts were entering old age as mortality reduced older cohorts, yet the population at ages most likely to need intensive health and care services grew sharply.

−2.60%children under 15
−0.27%working-age population
+2.26%people aged 75+

This is why a rising foreign population cannot be described simply as a replacement. Many foreign residents are of working age, which can ease labor shortages, support tax revenue and keep services operating. Yet 325,000 additional residents in one year do not reverse a shrinking child population, rebuild local birth cohorts, or instantly create enough nurses, homes and transport for a rapidly growing oldest-old population.

What changes on the street

Demographic change becomes visible first in ordinary places: a convenience store shift, a factory dormitory, a rural hotel, a language desk at city hall, a classroom receiving a child who speaks another language at home. Employers recruit abroad because vacancies are real. Municipalities translate procedures because residents need them. Schools and hospitals adapt because diversity is no longer confined to central Tokyo.

The national label “foreign population” also hides people with very different lives: students, technical workers, highly skilled professionals, spouses, children born or raised in Japan, and permanent residents. Treating them as a single temporary labor reserve misses the policy question. If Japan depends on newcomers for the long term, integration is infrastructure, not hospitality.

The 3.974 million total is a count of foreign nationals in the population estimate, not a count of everyone in Japan with an international background. A naturalized Japanese citizen is counted as Japanese. A child’s experience may be multilingual even when the nationality column cannot show it. Conversely, a registered foreign resident may be in Japan for a limited period. Nationality data are useful, but they are not a complete map of identity, belonging or future settlement.

That distinction matters politically. A government can raise worker intake while continuing to describe the change as temporary. Employers can recruit people without the town expanding language support or housing access. The population table records the result after those decisions meet real life. It cannot tell us whether institutions are ready, but its pace makes delay harder to defend.

That means predictable residence pathways, enforceable workplace rights, Japanese-language education, multilingual medical access, housing without discrimination and schooling that does not leave children translating adult bureaucracy. It also means allowing local communities to see foreign residents as neighbors with agency rather than as a number that plugs a labor-market hole.

What the number does not prove

The release does not show that immigration caused Japan’s population decline; births and deaths drive the natural decrease. It does not show that every region is changing at the same pace. It does not prove that a larger foreign population automatically raises productivity or that it lowers wages. Those questions require labor, migration and prefectural data.

Nor does the number make family policy irrelevant. Immigration and support for births are not substitutes. Affordable housing, stable employment, childcare and working hours influence whether people can form the families they want. Migration policy influences whether newcomers can build secure lives. Japan needs to manage both because the age structure was built over decades and will not turn quickly.

The long horizon

The National Institute of Population and Social Security Research’s 2023 projection runs to 2070. Its middle assumptions do not forecast a sudden demographic cliff; they describe a long slope. Projections change when fertility, mortality and migration assumptions change, but their value is to expose the scale and time lag of decisions.

A smaller population is not automatically a poorer society. Productivity, health, technology, compact urban planning and the distribution of work can protect living standards. But adaptation has costs. Empty homes do not teleport to the cities where workers need them. A closed school does not become a care facility without staff and money. A train line cannot keep its old frequency when its passenger base disappears.

There is also no single national solution because demographic geography is uneven. A Tokyo ward worried about crowded schools and multilingual services faces a different problem from a mountain town worried about its last bus, clinic and supermarket. National totals should guide financing and migration rules; local data must guide where services merge, where housing is reused and where a community decides that access matters more than preserving every old boundary.

That is the more useful way to read 530,000. It is not merely a ranking or a national mood. It is an annual change in the number of people available to live in houses, ride buses, pay taxes, raise children, staff hospitals and care for parents. The foreign-population rise shows that Japan is already responding through human movement, whether political language has caught up or not.

The word jinkō—population—looks like one total. This release shows why it should be read as a composition. Japan has fewer people, far fewer children, more residents over 75, and a rapidly growing foreign community. All four facts are true at once. Any policy that speaks to only one of them is describing a country that no longer exists.
